looks_like_me_why: There's a decent likeness in hair mass, general face shape and smile — the 3D 'Red' reads as you at a glance. But it's heavily stylized (childified Pixar look) so age, proportions and small ID cues are lost: no nose stud, brows/eyes are exaggerated, and facial proportions wobble from page to page (some pages read older, some very childlike). Pages where it reads best: cover, pages 3–4, 9. Pages where the face drifts off-model: 6 (eyes too wide), 11–13 (expressions look older/more angular), 14–15 (panic expressions feel like a different face).
rings_true_why: Narrative beats and pacing follow the classic tale cleanly — clear beginning, obstacle, climax, rescue and tidy moral. Image staging sells the story (establishing shots, close-ups, action spread). It reads like a picture-book retelling, but the text treatment is generic and the woodcutter/grandma reveal could use stronger connective beats (a couple of turns feel abrupt).
professional_why: Rendering, color and lighting are high-quality — polished 3D look, strong color keys, charming production design. BUT as an art director I see problems that stop this from being 'publish-ready': on-model inconsistency, several anatomy/hand issues, awkward basket/hand interaction, sometimes sloppy perspective (feet/ground contact), and zero typographic design — text is pasted-on. For a commercial printed product I'd want fixes before paying/buying as a finished book.
not_good: Consistency: character model drifts across pages (face proportions, hair length, missing nose stud) — pages 6, 11–13, 14–15. Hands and grips: Red's hands are stiff or float through props on pages 3, 6 and 12; wolf paw anatomy inconsistent (overly human finger shapes vs paw pads) on pages 5, 11, 13–14. Perspective/grounding: uneven foot contact/weight on pages 4, 7 and 14. Anatomy/expression: some panic poses look like a different character (pages 14–15). Composition/typography: text is unintegrated — risky over busy backgrounds (esp. pages 1, 7, 9). Also the wardrobe/Grandma reveal feels narratively thin — why a wardrobe? needs a visual hint earlier (page 8–10).
liked: Love the production design — cottage, quilt, props, florals, and the warm evening palette. Lighting and atmosphere are excellent; compositions have good silhouette and clear focal points in most spreads (cover, pages 4, 8, 18). The wolf design is expressive and the humor/tension beats read well. With tighter character consistency, fixed hands and a considered typographic layout this could be a very sweet, giftable picture book.
